items.stem: Which term describes the shared way of life of a group, including its norms, values, beliefs, language and material objects, passed from one generation to the next?
items.answer: Culture
items.markingKey: Culture: the shared way of life of a group, including its norms, values, beliefs, language and material objects, passed from one generation to the next. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “norms”, and give one example.
items.answer: Specific, informal rules or expectations about how people should behave in particular situations. Example: queuing in a shop or shaking hands when meeting someone.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (specific, informal rules or expectations about how people should behave in particular situations); 1 mark for a relevant example such as queuing in a shop or shaking hands when meeting someone. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “role” and “values”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Role: the set of expected behaviours attached to a particular position in society (e.g. the role of a teacher, which involves teaching and caring for pupils). Values: general beliefs about what is good, right and worth striving for in a society (e.g. respect for elders or the importance of individual achievement).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In Manila, a young woman who is a full-time nurse, a mother and a carer for her elderly father says she “cannot be in three places at once”. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: socialisation passes on the shared norms and values of society, creating value consensus and preparing individuals for adult roles; agencies such as the family and school integrate the individual into society (Parsons, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Hana, who has recently moved to Seoul, is unsure whether to bow, shake hands or kiss on the cheek when meeting colleagues. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: socialisation passes on the shared norms and values of society, creating value consensus and preparing individuals for adult roles; agencies such as the family and school integrate the individual into society (Parsons, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) to research changing attitudes towards achieved and ascribed status.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they can combine quantitative and qualitative data. Limitations: being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changing attitudes towards achieved and ascribed status but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the shared way of life of a group, including its norms, values, beliefs, language and material objects, passed from one generation to the next?
items.answer: Culture
items.markingKey: Culture: the shared way of life of a group, including its norms, values, beliefs, language and material objects, passed from one generation to the next. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “ascribed status”?
items.answer: A social position given at birth or fixed by characteristics a person cannot change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a social position given at birth or fixed by characteristics a person cannot change. [1]

items.stem: A sociologist in Accra wants to research the norms and values of a youth subculture in Doha. Explain one strength of using case studies for this research.
items.answer: A single case can give rare insight into an unusual or closed group.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the norms and values of a youth subculture in Doha. [2]

items.stem: In Hanoi, a young woman who is a full-time nurse, a mother and a carer for her elderly father says she “cannot be in three places at once”. Compare how interactionist and functionalist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: socialisation is an active, two-way process: individuals interpret and negotiate the norms and roles they are taught, and the self develops through interaction with significant others (Mead, Cooley). Functionalism: socialisation passes on the shared norms and values of society, creating value consensus and preparing individuals for adult roles; agencies such as the family and school integrate the individual into society (Parsons, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Tariq, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on attitudes to status and success in Santiago. The report was based on 450 adults. Table: percentage agreeing that “success depends mainly on hard work rather than family background” | 2000 | 2025. People aged 18-34 | 58% | 67%. People aged 35-59 | 60% | 68%. People aged 60+ | 42% | 48%. (a) Suppose 300 of the respondents were People aged 35-59. Using the 2025 figure, calculate how many of them gave this response. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that achieved status has replaced ascribed status in modern societies.
items.answer: (a) 68% of 300 = 68 ÷ 100 × 300 = 204 (to the nearest whole person). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for People aged 18-34, People aged 35-59, People aged 60+; People aged 35-59 had the highest figure for 2025. Younger people have grown up with wider access to education and may believe positions are earned. Qualifications: Beliefs are not the same as reality: social mobility studies show family background still strongly affects life chances; ascribed characteristics such as gender, ethnicity and caste still matter. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 450 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method (68 ÷ 100 × 300); 1 mark answer 204. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the lifelong process by which people learn the culture (norms, values and roles) of their society?
items.answer: Socialisation
items.markingKey: Socialisation: the lifelong process by which people learn the culture (norms, values and roles) of their society. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “hidden curriculum”, and give one example.
items.answer: The norms, values and attitudes that schools teach informally through their organisation and routines, rather than through formal lessons. Example: learning punctuality and respect for authority.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the norms, values and attitudes that schools teach informally through their organisation and routines, rather than through formal lessons); 1 mark for a relevant example such as learning punctuality and respect for authority. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “role model” and “peer group”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Role model: a person whose behaviour is copied by others, especially children (e.g. a child copying an older sibling or a sports star). Peer group: a group of people of similar age and status who influence each other’s behaviour (e.g. teenage friends who share fashion and music tastes).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Ana, aged 14, starts dressing and speaking like a group of older students at school in Dhaka and stops spending time with family at weekends. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: socialisation transmits ruling-class ideology, teaching people to accept hierarchy and inequality as normal; agencies such as education and the media reproduce capitalist values and false class consciousness (Althusser).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Parents in Colombo give their son toy cars and praise him for being “tough”, while they buy their daughter dolls and praise her for being “kind”. Explain how a liberal feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: gender socialisation teaches boys and girls different, unequal roles; changing socialisation (non-sexist toys, books and teaching) can reduce gender inequality (Oakley).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Ana, aged 14, starts dressing and speaking like a group of older students at school in Auckland and stops spending time with family at weekends. Compare how liberal feminist and Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: gender socialisation teaches boys and girls different, unequal roles; changing socialisation (non-sexist toys, books and teaching) can reduce gender inequality (Oakley). Marxism: socialisation transmits ruling-class ideology, teaching people to accept hierarchy and inequality as normal; agencies such as education and the media reproduce capitalist values and false class consciousness (Althusser).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to research how parents socialise young children into gender roles.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewee can raise issues the researcher had not thought of, so the research is not limited by pre-set categories; they produce rich, detailed qualitative data that gives verstehen (an empathetic understanding). Limitations: the power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear; samples are small, so findings are difficult to generalise. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how parents socialise young children into gender roles but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful laboratory experiments are for studying the hidden curriculum in a secondary school.
items.answer: Strengths: the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability; results are quantitative and easy to compare. Limitations: it is impossible to control all the variables that affect human behaviour; the artificial setting means people may not behave as they would in real life, so validity is low. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the hidden curriculum in a secondary school but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the early socialisation of children, mainly by the family, in which basic norms, values and language are learnt?
items.answer: Primary socialisation
items.markingKey: Primary socialisation: the early socialisation of children, mainly by the family, in which basic norms, values and language are learnt. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “peer group”.
items.answer: A group of people of similar age and status who influence each other’s behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a group of people of similar age and status who influence each other’s behaviour. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “agency of socialisation” and “peer group”.
items.answer: Agency of socialisation: a group or institution that teaches people the norms and values of society. Peer group: a group of people of similar age and status who influence each other’s behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Daniel, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on influences on young people in Nairobi. The report was based on 400 young people aged 13-17. Table: percentage naming this as the “biggest influence on my opinions” | 2010 | 2025. Parents | 46% | 42%. Friends | 26% | 32%. Social media | 9% | 17%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Friends change between 2010 and 2025?
items.answer: +6 percentage points
items.markingKey: 32 − 26 = +6 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Daniel, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on influences on young people in Istanbul. The report was based on 600 young people aged 13-17. Table: percentage naming this as the “biggest influence on my opinions” | 2010 | 2025. Parents | 49% | 35%. Friends | 23% | 27%. Social media | 7% | 26%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Parents between 2010 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the family is no longer the most important agency of socialisation.
items.answer: (a) (35 − 49) ÷ 49 × 100 = -28.6%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Friends, Social media; the figure fell for Parents; Parents had the highest figure for 2025. The growth of social media has made it a powerful agency of secondary socialisation. Qualifications: Parents are still the most named influence for many; primary socialisation in early childhood shapes how young people interpret later influences; self-reports by teenagers may underestimate family influence. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 600 young people aged 13-17 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (35 − 49) ÷ 49 × 100; 1 mark for -28.6% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of influences on young people (400 young people aged 13-17, Lima). Table: percentage naming this as the “biggest influence on my opinions” | 2010 | 2025. Parents | 57% | 47%. Friends | 22% | 21%. Social media | 8% | 20%. (a) Calculate the gap between Parents and Friends in 2010 and in 2025, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Explain one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the family is no longer the most important agency of socialisation.
items.answer: (a) 2010: 35 percentage points; 2025: 26 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) Younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Social media; the figure fell for Parents, Friends; Parents had the highest figure for 2025. Postmodernists argue young people draw on many global influences rather than only the family. Qualifications: Parents are still the most named influence for many; primary socialisation in early childhood shapes how young people interpret later influences; self-reports by teenagers may underestimate family influence. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 400 young people aged 13-17 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (35 and 26); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that human behaviour is mainly determined by biological or genetic factors?
items.answer: Nature
items.markingKey: Nature: the view that human behaviour is mainly determined by biological or genetic factors. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “feral children”, and give one example.
items.answer: Children who have grown up with little or no human contact and so have not been socialised. Example: children found living with animals or locked away from society.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (children who have grown up with little or no human contact and so have not been socialised); 1 mark for a relevant example such as children found living with animals or locked away from society. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “nature” and “nurture”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Nature: the view that human behaviour is mainly determined by biological or genetic factors (e.g. claims that aggression is caused by male hormones). Nurture: the view that human behaviour is mainly shaped by socialisation and the social environment (e.g. children learning language and customs from those around them).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A newspaper in Santiago reports the discovery of a seven-year-old child who had been kept alone in a room and had never learnt to speak. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: behaviour is shaped by socialisation into shared norms and values; without primary socialisation a person cannot take on social roles, showing the importance of nurture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In one society women do most farming while men care for children; in another society near Dhaka the roles are reversed. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: behaviour is shaped by socialisation into shared norms and values; without primary socialisation a person cannot take on social roles, showing the importance of nurture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Noah is planning a study of how children who have experienced extreme neglect develop language. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how children who have experienced extreme neglect develop language but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “cultural relativism”?
items.answer: The idea that behaviour should be understood in relation to the culture in which it occurs, not judged by the standards of another culture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the idea that behaviour should be understood in relation to the culture in which it occurs, not judged by the standards of another culture. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “feral children” and “nurture”.
items.answer: Feral children: children who have grown up with little or no human contact and so have not been socialised. Nurture: the view that human behaviour is mainly shaped by socialisation and the social environment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Sofia, a sociology student, is designing a project on how children who have experienced extreme neglect develop language. Explain one limitation of using non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: The presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how children who have experienced extreme neglect develop language. [2]

items.stem: Two siblings separated at birth are raised in different countries; one becomes a confident public speaker and the other is shy and reserved. Explain how functionalist and interactionist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: behaviour is shaped by socialisation into shared norms and values; without primary socialisation a person cannot take on social roles, showing the importance of nurture. Interactionism: the self develops through interaction with others; lack of interaction means the self, language and the ability to take the role of the other cannot develop (Mead).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes specific, informal rules or expectations about how people should behave in particular situations?
items.answer: Norms
items.markingKey: Norms: specific, informal rules or expectations about how people should behave in particular situations. [1]

items.stem: State one reason why culture is said to be learnt rather than inherited.
items.answer: Children raised in a different culture adopt its norms and language.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. children raised in a different culture adopt its norms and language. [1]

items.stem: Linton argued that every society distinguishes between ascribed and achieved statuses. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Linton argued that statuses are positions in society with attached roles; ascribed statuses are fixed at birth and achieved statuses are earned. Criticism: Critics argue many “achieved” statuses still depend heavily on ascribed characteristics such as class and ethnicity.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Functionalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of attitudes to status and success (300 adults, Istanbul). Table: percentage agreeing that “success depends mainly on hard work rather than family background” | 2000 | 2025. People aged 18-34 | 70% | 72%. People aged 35-59 | 50% | 50%. People aged 60+ | 40% | 46%. By how many percentage points did the figure for People aged 18-34 change between 2000 and 2025?
items.answer: +2 percentage points
items.markingKey: 72 − 70 = +2 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A sociologist in Colombo wants to research changing attitudes towards achieved and ascribed status. Explain two limitations of using self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: 1. Respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. 2. Response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to changing attitudes towards achieved and ascribed status. [4]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which culture influences human behaviour.
items.answer: Norms guide behaviour in specific situations and are enforced by sanctions; values shape goals and choices; roles give expectations attached to statuses; language and beliefs shape how people see the world.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Norms guide behaviour in specific situations and are enforced by sanctions; values shape goals and choices; roles give expectations attached to statuses; language and beliefs shape how people see the world. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes socialisation that continues beyond the family, through agencies such as schools, peer groups, the media, religion and the workplace?
items.answer: Secondary socialisation
items.markingKey: Secondary socialisation: socialisation that continues beyond the family, through agencies such as schools, peer groups, the media, religion and the workplace. [1]

items.stem: State one way in which schools socialise pupils.
items.answer: By teaching shared national history and values.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. by teaching shared national history and values. [1]

items.stem: Oakley argued that gender socialisation takes place through manipulation and canalisation. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Oakley argued that parents manipulate children’s self-concept by encouraging gender-appropriate behaviour and canalise them towards gender-typed toys and activities. Criticism: Critics argue that children today experience much more varied gender socialisation and choose their own identities.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Liberal feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Tariq, a sociology student, is designing a project on the hidden curriculum in a secondary school. Explain one strength of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: The interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the hidden curriculum in a secondary school. [2]

items.stem: A survey of 300 young people aged 13-17 in Hanoi produced the data below. Table: percentage naming this as the “biggest influence on my opinions” | 2010 | 2025. Parents | 48% | 39%. Friends | 29% | 27%. Social media | 8% | 24%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Parents change between 2010 and 2025?
items.answer: -9 percentage points
items.markingKey: 39 − 48 = -9 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: The table shows results from research into influences on young people, using self-completion questionnaires with 1200 young people aged 13-17 in Jakarta. Table: percentage naming this as the “biggest influence on my opinions” | 2010 | 2025. Parents | 50% | 40%. Friends | 22% | 26%. Social media | 11% | 25%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Social media between 2010 and 2025. (b) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Social media between 2010 and 2025. Show your working.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 11 and 25; 1 mark for +14 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for (25 − 11) ÷ 11 × 100; 1 mark for 127.3% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2]

items.stem: Study the following extract (Source A) from a report on research carried out in Lisbon. “A researcher observed 25 families with young children in Bangkok, visiting each home twice a week for a month. She noted that parents usually praised girls for being helpful and boys for being brave. Several parents said they “treated their children the same”, but their behaviour often differed.” (a) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that the family is the most important agency of gender socialisation.
items.answer: (a) 1. Parents praised girls for being helpful and boys for being brave. 2. Parents claimed to treat children the same but their behaviour often differed. (b) For: The source shows parents shaping gendered behaviour from an early age; primary socialisation is highly influential (Oakley, Parsons). Against: Schools, peers and the media also teach gender norms; children actively negotiate identities; the observer’s presence may have changed parents’ behaviour and 25 families in one city are not representative. Also consider how far a single study using non-participant observation can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Source A: “A researcher observed 25 families with young children in Kathmandu, visiting each home twice a week for a month. She noted that parents usually praised girls for being helpful and boys for being brave. Several parents said they “treated their children the same”, but their behaviour often differed.” Use Source A and your own knowledge to answer the questions. (a) Using Source A, explain one strength of the method used for studying gender socialisation in families. (b) Explain how a liberal feminist sociologist might interpret the findings in Source A. (c) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that the family is the most important agency of gender socialisation.
items.answer: (a) Children can be observed in classrooms or playgrounds without having to answer questions. (b) The findings show gender socialisation through manipulation (praise for gender-appropriate behaviour), as Oakley argued; changing parents’ practices could reduce inequality. (c) For: The source shows parents shaping gendered behaviour from an early age; primary socialisation is highly influential (Oakley, Parsons). Against: Schools, peers and the media also teach gender norms; children actively negotiate identities; the observer’s presence may have changed parents’ behaviour and 25 families in one city are not representative. Also consider how far a single study using non-participant observation can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant strength; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the findings in the source. [3] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that human behaviour is mainly determined by biological or genetic factors?
items.answer: Nature
items.markingKey: Nature: the view that human behaviour is mainly determined by biological or genetic factors. [1]

items.stem: Outline what Murdock meant by arguing that some social institutions, such as the nuclear family, are universal because they meet basic needs.
items.answer: Murdock studied over 200 societies and argued the nuclear family was found in all of them, performing sexual, reproductive, economic and educational functions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Murdock studied over 200 societies and argued the nuclear family was found in all of them, performing sexual, reproductive, economic and educational functions. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “cultural relativism” and “biological determinism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Cultural relativism: the idea that behaviour should be understood in relation to the culture in which it occurs, not judged by the standards of another culture (e.g. understanding different marriage customs in their own cultural context). Biological determinism: the belief that biology fixes human behaviour and social differences (e.g. claims that women are naturally better suited to childcare).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: The table shows time-use data from 240 households in three countries, collected by Leila’s research team. Table: average daily minutes spent on childcare | Fathers | Mothers. Country A | 17 min | 57 min. Country B | 30 min | 47 min. Country C | 40 min | 45 min. What is the difference, in minutes, between Fathers and Mothers for Country A (Mothers minus Fathers)?
items.answer: +40 minutes

items.stem: Yusuf, a sociology student, is designing a project on gender roles in two contrasting cultures. Explain two strengths of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning. 2. The interviewer can probe and clarify answers, which improves validity.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to gender roles in two contrasting cultures. [4]

items.stem: Kenji, a sociology student, is designing a project on how children who have experienced extreme neglect develop language. Evaluate the use of laboratory experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability; the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified. Limitations: it would be unethical to recreate harmful situations, such as violence, in a laboratory; it is impossible to control all the variables that affect human behaviour. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how children who have experienced extreme neglect develop language but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes general beliefs about what is good, right and worth striving for in a society?
items.answer: Values
items.markingKey: Values: general beliefs about what is good, right and worth striving for in a society. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “norms”?
items.answer: Specific, informal rules or expectations about how people should behave in particular situations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: specific, informal rules or expectations about how people should behave in particular situations. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between norms and values, using an example of each.
items.answer: Values are general beliefs about what is desirable (e.g. respect for privacy); norms are specific rules of behaviour that put values into practice (e.g. knocking before entering a room).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark each example; must show the link that norms express values. [4]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of attitudes to status and success (1000 adults, Manila). Table: percentage agreeing that “success depends mainly on hard work rather than family background” | 2000 | 2025. People aged 18-34 | 65% | 75%. People aged 35-59 | 53% | 58%. People aged 60+ | 40% | 39%. By how many percentage points did the figure for People aged 35-59 change between 2000 and 2025?
items.answer: +5 percentage points
items.markingKey: 58 − 53 = +5 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A group of young skateboarders in Nairobi have their own slang, clothing style and rules about who belongs. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: socialisation passes on the shared norms and values of society, creating value consensus and preparing individuals for adult roles; agencies such as the family and school integrate the individual into society (Parsons, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying the norms and values of a youth subculture in Cape Town.
items.answer: Strengths: there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the norms and values of a youth subculture in Cape Town but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a group or institution that teaches people the norms and values of society?
items.answer: Agency of socialisation
items.markingKey: Agency of socialisation: a group or institution that teaches people the norms and values of society. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “role model”.
items.answer: A person whose behaviour is copied by others, especially children.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a person whose behaviour is copied by others, especially children. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which the peer group acts as an agency of socialisation.
items.answer: Peers use informal sanctions (approval, teasing, exclusion) to enforce group norms; they provide role models for style, language and attitudes; they can encourage conformity or deviance through peer pressure.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each way explained (identification + development). [4]

items.stem: Parents in Cairo give their son toy cars and praise him for being “tough”, while they buy their daughter dolls and praise her for being “kind”. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: people now choose from a wide range of global cultural influences, especially through the media, so socialisation is more fragmented and identities are more fluid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of influences on young people (300 young people aged 13-17, Bangkok). Table: percentage naming this as the “biggest influence on my opinions” | 2010 | 2025. Parents | 47% | 37%. Friends | 29% | 30%. Social media | 15% | 25%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Friends change between 2010 and 2025?
items.answer: +1 percentage point
items.markingKey: 30 − 29 = +1 percentage point. [1]

items.stem: The table shows results from research into influences on young people, using self-completion questionnaires with 600 young people aged 13-17 in Colombo. Table: percentage naming this as the “biggest influence on my opinions” | 2010 | 2025. Parents | 48% | 41%. Friends | 23% | 25%. Social media | 13% | 30%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for 2025. (b) Calculate the gap between Parents and Social media in 2010 and in 2025, and state whether it narrowed or widened.
items.answer: (a) Parents (41%). (b) 2010: 35 percentage points; 2025: 11 percentage points; the gap narrowed.
items.markingKey: (a) Parents, 41%. [1] (b) 1 mark each gap (35 and 11); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which secondary agencies of socialisation shape identity.
items.answer: Education: formal and hidden curriculum, labelling, gender subject choice; peer groups: informal sanctions and subcultural identities; media: role models and representations; religion: moral values and community identity; workplace: occupational norms.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Education: formal and hidden curriculum, labelling, gender subject choice; peer groups: informal sanctions and subcultural identities; media: role models and representations; religion: moral values and community identity; workplace: occupational norms. [8]

items.stem: A survey of 450 young people aged 13-17 in Dhaka produced the data below. Table: percentage naming this as the “biggest influence on my opinions” | 2010 | 2025. Parents | 54% | 46%. Friends | 22% | 25%. Social media | 11% | 27%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Friends between 2010 and 2025. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of influences on young people. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the family is no longer the most important agency of socialisation.
items.answer: (a) 25 − 22 = +3 percentage points. (b) They measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Friends, Social media; the figure fell for Parents; Parents had the highest figure for 2025. Postmodernists argue young people draw on many global influences rather than only the family. Qualifications: Parents are still the most named influence for many; primary socialisation in early childhood shapes how young people interpret later influences; self-reports by teenagers may underestimate family influence. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 450 young people aged 13-17 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 22 and 25; 1 mark for +3 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that human behaviour is mainly shaped by socialisation and the social environment?
items.answer: Nurture
items.markingKey: Nurture: the view that human behaviour is mainly shaped by socialisation and the social environment. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Feral children prove that biology has no influence on human behaviour.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They show socialisation is essential, but they do not rule out biological influences; most sociologists see nature and nurture interacting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Curtiss argued that the case of Genie showed that a child deprived of human contact during early childhood could not fully acquire language. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Genie, discovered aged 13 after years of isolation, learnt some words but never mastered grammar, suggesting a critical period for socialisation. Criticism: Single cases may be untypical: Genie may have had developmental problems from birth, and she suffered severe abuse.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Researchers compared time-use diaries from 1200 households in three countries. Table: average daily minutes spent on childcare | Fathers | Mothers. Country A | 12 min | 44 min. Country B | 34 min | 56 min. Country C | 45 min | 55 min. What is the difference, in minutes, between Fathers and Mothers for Country B (Mothers minus Fathers)?
items.answer: +22 minutes

items.stem: A newspaper in Hanoi reports the discovery of a seven-year-old child who had been kept alone in a room and had never learnt to speak. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: the self develops through interaction with others; lack of interaction means the self, language and the ability to take the role of the other cannot develop (Mead).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying gender roles in two contrasting cultures.
items.answer: Strengths: they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying gender roles in two contrasting cultures but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]
